claim: Only the Palestinians became refugees in 1948.

heard.who: Yated Ne'eman, an anti-Zionist ultra-Orthodox Israeli newspaper, quoted by Yehouda Shenhav
heard.quote: this talk about 'Jewish refugees who were expelled from Arab countries' as opposed to 'Arab refugees who were expelled from the land of Israel' was grating to our journalistic ears

heard.who: Shlomo Hillel, Israeli minister and organiser of the Iraqi Jews' departure, quoted by Yehouda Shenhav (1998)
heard.quote: I do not regard the exodus of Jews from Arab countries as refugees.

answer: Palestinians were not the only people displaced in these years. Around 800,000 to 850,000 Jews lived in Arab countries and Iran in the late 1940s, and most of them left over the next two or three decades. About 600,000 went to Israel; others went to France, Britain and the Americas. Reasons differ by country: persecution and expulsion in some, organised emigration and a wish to go to Israel in others. The numbers are estimates, mostly from Israeli and Jewish organisations. Some Israeli Jews themselves, such as Shlomo Hillel, reject the word refugee for their own departure. This is not an equation. One displacement does not cancel the other.

facts.text: Estimates put the Jewish population of Arab and Muslim countries around 1948 at roughly 800,000 to 850,000.

sources.publisher: Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.title: Refugees: Jewish
sources.quote: an estimated 800,000 Jews living in Arab and Muslim countries were subjected to anti-Jewish violence, abuse, and persecution

sources.title: Fact Sheet: Jewish Refugees from Arab Countries

facts.text: Most left between 1948 and the early 1970s. One advocacy count gives 820,000 departures from 1948 to 1972, of whom 586,000 went to Israel. In Iraq, 123,370 were airlifted in 1950 to 1951.

sources.title: Fact Sheet: Jewish Refugees from Arab Countries
sources.quote: of the 820,000 Jewish refugees between 1948 and 1972, more than 200,000 found refuge in Europe and North America while 586,000 were resettled in Israel

sources.publisher: Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.title: Refugees: Jewish
sources.quote: Between 1950 and 1951, 123,370 Iraqi Jews were airlifted to Israel in Operation Ezra and Nehemiah

facts.text: Experiences varied. Iraq allowed its 160,000 Jews to leave in 1950 if they gave up their nationality and unsold property; Shlomo Hillel, who helped organise that exodus, later said he did not count it as refugee flight.

sources.publisher: Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.title: Refugees: Jewish
sources.quote: the Iraqi government permitted its 160,000 Jews to emigrate provided they renounced their Iraqi nationality and whatever properties and assets they could not sell

sources.quote: I do not regard the exodus of Jews from Arab countries as refugees. I do not accept that.

facts.text: Scholars and advocates debate the label. Shenhav calls describing these Jews as refugees reasonable given post-war usage of the term; advocacy sources state it flatly.

sources.publisher: British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies (Yehouda Shenhav, 2002)
sources.title: Jews from Arab Countries and the Palestinian Right for Return
sources.quote: the description of the Jews from Arab lands as refugees was not unreasonable in the light of the fact that the term "refugee" became a central concept

sources.title: Fact Sheet: Jewish Refugees from Arab Countries
sources.quote: the Jews of the Arab world fled their homes as refugees

facts.text: The Jewish refugee claim has been used to argue against Palestinian return and compensation. An Israeli organisation of Jews from Arab countries registered Jewish property left behind for that purpose, among others.

sources.publisher: Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East and North Africa (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.title: Refugees: Jewish
sources.quote: in order, possibly, to make future demands for restitution or to offset Palestinian Arab demands for property left behind in Israel in 1948

sources.publisher: British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies (Yehouda Shenhav, 2002)
sources.title: Jews from Arab Countries and the Palestinian Right for Return
sources.quote: to counterbalance the claims of the Palestinian leadership on the right to the land and on the refugee question

contested: Numbers: the totals come from Israeli and Jewish organisations and encyclopedia estimates (800,000, 820,000, 851,000); they are estimates, not census counts of departures, and no single agreed figure exists.

The word refugee: some leaders of the Israeli community from Arab lands, such as Shlomo Hillel, reject it for their own departure; the ultra-Orthodox paper Yated Ne'eman argued the migration was Zionist immigration and not deportation. Shenhav's article argues the term was adopted in the 1970s largely to counter Palestinian claims.
Causes differ by country and period: expulsion and legal discrimination in some places, organised emigration and Zionist motives in others. Sources do not agree on the share of each.
not_claimed: This card does not say Jewish displacement cancels out Palestinian displacement, or that one makes the other acceptable.
It does not claim every Jew who left an Arab country was expelled.
It does not claim the Arab states acted on one plan; it records different cases.
It does not give a settled number; all figures here are estimates, mostly from Israeli and Jewish organisations.
